coach_says: You're a piece down in any case, and Nh5+ changes very little. The real worry is the white knight on d5, which hits e7 and threatens Nc7, forking both your rooks. Trading it off with Nxd5+ was the tidier choice, but the check you played doesn't lose anything important.

Good, taking the knight back on c8 was the right call and the engine's first choice. The knight had nowhere safe to go, and taking it got back a lot of the material you'd lost. Next, look after your bishops on d4 and c4, which are both under attack.

The damage happened earlier, when the knight went to h4 and got cut off. Here Nf3 saves the knight but lets the bishop on b1 escape with Be4. Bb5, pinning the c6 knight while you develop, was a bit more useful, but every option leaves you about a piece down.

White's bishop on d8 is in trouble: your king attacks it and only the queen on h4 defends it. Be7 attacks the queen but lets White swap that stranded bishop with Bxe7, and their problem is gone. Bd6 was stronger because it also guards c7, so the bishop on d8 has no target and must waste a move retreating, and you keep the extra pawn and a lead in development. When the opponent has a stranded piece, don't offer to trade it for them.

In a rook endgame your king should head where it does damage. Kf4 aims for e3, close to White's king on g1, so your rook can check and attack from the first and second ranks. Kf5 is a passive square that does nothing to stop b4 and a4 opening the queenside, and most of your advantage is gone. Ask yourself which squares bring your king closer to their king or pawns.
also: box in the king on the back rank

coach_says: Your knight on g3 was under attack from the bishop on f4 and the pawn on f2, and g5 does nothing about it. White simply plays Bxg3 and your extra piece is gone. Before you start your own attack, check whether any of your pieces is attacked; Nf5 saved the knight and kept you a piece up.

Your king is caught in a mating net, and Kg7 just walks back into it: after Nh5+ it must go back to h6, because g8, f8, f7 and h8 are all covered or blocked, and then Bc1+ wins. Rf8 was the defence. It clears h8 so your king has somewhere to run after Bc1+ and Nh5+, and it puts your rook on the f-file against the f6 knight and the queen behind it. When your king is being hunted, make escape squares and hit the attacking pieces.
concept: make an escape square for the king

coach_says: Black's queen on d3 attacks your rook on f1 along the diagonal, and nothing defends it. Qf3 doesn't help because your own pawn on f2 blocks it, so Black takes the rook with check. After every enemy move, ask what it attacks; moving the rook to e1, d1 or g1 kept you winning.

Your b3 pawn is attacked twice, by the queen on b5 and the rook on b8, and defended only once, by your queen. Ba7 hits the rook, but Black takes on b3 anyway and the rook gets away, so you lose a pawn for nothing. Count attackers and defenders first; Qc2 adds a defender and also eyes c7.

White's rook is about to come to g1 on the open g-file, straight at your king. Bg5 blocks the file, but after Rg1 the bishop is pinned to your king and attacked by the rook, the queen and the c1 bishop, so White wins it. Kh8 first takes the king off the g-file, and then Rg8 fights for it. Get your king off an open file before the rook arrives.

Your king is still on e1 with the bishop on f1 undeveloped, and Black's queen is waiting to check on b4. c4 makes it worse: you can no longer block with c3, so after Qb4+ Rd2 Qb1+ Rd1 Black takes e4 with check and then the rook on h1. Bb5 develops, blocks the e-file and lets your king step to f1 and g1. When your king is in the middle, finish development and get it safe before you push pawns.
also: queen checks pick up loose pieces

coach_says: Your bishop on f1 was the only piece guarding g2 from Black's queen on g6. Bd3 attacks the queen, but the queen just takes on g2 and now hits your rook on h1, so you lose a pawn and your kingside gets messy. Before you move a piece, check what it was defending. Bg3 or Nf3 kept everything covered.
also: attacking the queen where it can take

coach_says: White is ready for fxe5: after dxe5, the bishop on c3 aims straight at your e5 pawn. a4 chases the bishop on b3, but White swaps it on e6 and then wins e5 because nothing can guard it any more. Bxb3 followed by Re8 keeps e5 defended. Before you chase a piece, check whether your opponent already has a threat in the centre.
also: chasing a piece that just trades

coach_says: d5 opens the centre while your king is still on e8 and your kingside pieces are undeveloped. After exd5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Ng5, White hits f7 and d5 at the same time and threatens Re1+ down the open e-file. Finish developing and castle (Be7 then O-O) before you break open the centre.
concept: opened the centre with king uncastled

coach_says: Black is threatening Qxg2 mate: the queen on g5 aims down the g-file and the knight on e3 also covers g2. h4 doesn't stop it. Whenever an enemy queen and knight point at the square in front of your castled king, deal with it first; g3 or Kf2 would have kept the game going.

Your king is on e1 with Black's rook on e8 and only Black's knight on e4 between them, so any knight move gives a discovered check. Taking on d5 ignores that, and Qb4+ Ke2 Nc5+ leads to mate. Qd4+ was the move: it checks, attacks the e4 knight and brings your queen back to defend. When your king sits on an open file behind an enemy piece, deal with that before grabbing pawns.

The knight on h6 threatens Nf7 mate: your king on h8 has no squares, because g8 and g7 are covered by the queen on g3 and your own knight blocks h7. a5 ignores it. Before every move, look for checks your opponent can give; Qh5, which covers f7, kept you winning.

You can win both the b7 and c7 pawns, but the order matters. Qxb7 comes with a threat on the a8 rook, so Black has to deal with it and Bxc7 follows. Taking on c7 first lets Black hit your bishop with Rc8 and gain time to organise, castling long or guarding b7. When there are two captures, take the one that makes a threat first.

Your rook on e7 is attacking the h7 pawn, and if you win it you can probably hold this rook ending. Kh2 or Kg2 gets out of check and keeps that threat. Kg4 walks into h5+, so Black's pawn moves with check onto a square the g6 pawn defends, and your chance to win it back is gone. When you get out of check, check where the enemy pawns can attack your king.
concept: let their h-pawn escape with check
also: win back pawns in rook endgames

coach_says: Your knight on b5 is attacked by the queen on a6, and it has a great escape: Nxc7 forks the queen on a6 and the rook on a8. Qb3+ lets Black block with Qe6 and offer a queen trade, so the fork only wins a pawn afterwards. With a knight near c7 and the king on f7, always check for forks on the queen and rook.
